lesson.title: Chez, the House Word
lesson.subtitle: chez Marie, chez le docteur, chez moi — the Latin casa preposition with no English twin.

hook.title: Why People Take chez Where Buildings Take à
hook.content: Before a person's name, profession, or stressed pronoun, French uses chez (from Latin casa 'house') to mean 'at/to someone's home or office': chez Marie, chez le docteur, chez moi, chez toi, chez nous!

footnotes.title: How chez covers both 'at' and 'to'
footnotes.content: Je suis chez moi ('I am at home') and Je vais chez moi ('I am going home') both use bare chez!

pattern.title: Building → au / à la; Person or Pronoun → chez
pattern.content: Pair chez with people, professions, and stressed pronouns.
pattern.linguist_note: Unstressed proclitic use of Latin casa reduced phonetically to Old French chies → modern chez /ʃe/.
pattern.trap_note: Never say *Je vais à Marie or *à chez moi — chez already means 'at/to the home of' all by itself!

exercises.prompt: Match each chez phrase with its English meaning:

matching_pairs.german: at our home / in our country

exercises.target_answer: at / to my home, at / to your place (informal), at / to his / her place, at our home / in our country, at / to the doctor's office
exercises.meaning: chez moi, chez toi, chez lui / chez elle, chez nous, chez le docteur
exercises.explanation: chez pairs with stressed pronouns or people/professions.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'I am staying at home tonight'?
options: Je reste chez moi ce soir
Je reste chez je ce soir
Je reste à moi ce soir
exercises.target_answer: Je reste chez moi ce soir
exercises.meaning: I am staying at home tonight
exercises.explanation: chez + stressed pronoun moi = 'at my home'.

exercises.prompt: What is the literal historical meaning of 'On dîne chez Marie'?
exercises.meaning: Literal structure: One dines at-the-house-of Marie
exercises.explanation: chez (from Latin casa) means 'at the house/place of'.

exercises.idea: are you going to the doctor's office today
cues: to the doctor's office today → chez le docteur aujourd'hui
idea_parts: person-destination + time → chez le docteur aujourd'hui
exercises.target_answer: Tu vas chez le docteur aujourd'hui
exercises.meaning: Are you going to the doctor's office today?
exercises.explanation: Because le docteur is a person, French uses chez le docteur rather than au.

diagnosis.cue: People and professions take chez: chez le docteur.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Je suis chez mon ami ce soir
exercises.target_answer: Je suis chez mon ami ce soir
exercises.meaning: I am at my friend's place tonight
exercises.explanation: chez mon ami = 'at my friend's home'.
exercises.affirmation: You used chez mon ami cleanly.

summary.outcome: Use chez with names, professions, and stressed pronouns for 'at/to someone's place'.

use_example.german: Tu viens chez moi ou on va chez toi ?
use_example.english: Are you coming to my place or are we going to yours?

summary.takeaway: Places take au / à la; people take chez.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([1303] The Partitive: du, de la & Negative de): see how Chez, the House Word leads directly into The Partitive: du, de la & Negative de.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "Are you going to the doctor's office today" in French:
twist.target_answer: Tu vas chez le docteur aujourd'hui
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Tu vas chez le docteur aujourd'hui" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of Chez, the House Word.

chez.etymology_derivation: Latin casa 'hut, house' — the same house English visits in casino (literally 'little house'). No English twin: an honest loss.

moi.etymology_derivation: Used after prepositions (avec moi, chez moi, pour moi) and in C'est moi.

toi.etymology_derivation: Used after prepositions: pour toi, chez toi.

lui.context_translation: I speak to him / to her.
lui.etymology_derivation: One single pronoun means BOTH 'to him' and 'to her' before a verb!

nous.etymology_derivation: Latin nōs — English keeps the root in nostrum.

vous.etymology_derivation: Latin vōs 'you all' promoted to politeness — the same T–V ladder as German Sie and English's lost 'ye'.

docteur.etymology_derivation: Latin doctor 'teacher'. -or/-er nouns convert to -eur and are usually masculine.

ami.etymology_derivation: In liaison, un ami sounds like /œ̃.na.mi/ and mes amis like /me.za.mi/.

rester.context_translation: I am going to stay here.
rester.etymology_derivation: Latin restāre (to stand back, remain). Takes être in the past (je suis resté).
